paras: The whipping of Hicks Smiley was an attack by a band of about twenty "regulators" on a Black man at his house near Gladdico, Tennessee, in the Cumberland River valley, in November 1888. The band tied Smiley to a tree, built a fire around him without letting the flames reach him, then whipped him and drove him back into his house. The attack became known through a Chattanooga dispatch about a regulator band said to be terrorizing Black residents of three counties, which papers across the country ran under headlines calling the band Ku-Klux.

According to J. A. Johnston, a traveling salesman for a Chattanooga wholesale grocery who had just returned from Smith, Jackson and Clay counties, a "veritable panic" existed there over a band of regulators "by whom negroes alone are molested." The band was said to have its headquarters at Carthage in Smith County, although others placed it at Tompkinsville, Kentucky, just across the state line. About two months earlier, notices ordering Black residents to leave or to stop "certain practices" had been chalked on their doors, particularly in the river bottoms, and had been ignored.

A score of men surrounded Smiley's house near Gladdico, called him out, tied him to a tree and built a fire around him. The flames were kept from touching him, though he was "heated up pretty well"; he was then released and driven into his house with a dozen licks of a whip on his legs. No accusation against Smiley himself was reported.

The same report described the band's other victims: the next night "Met" Tompkins, who lived four miles down the river, had his hair shaved and his back tarred and feathered, and was told to warn his "thieving neighbors." Watt Jenkins was given twenty lashes for alleged illegal possession of fowls and threatened with hanging, Molly Powell was tied to a mule and galloped up and down the road near Celina, and Henderson Duke, an elderly man near Carthage accused of stealing corn, was the most severely punished.

Black residents were said to be in "the greatest terror" and to insist that many of those punished were good citizens, while "the whites appear indifferent." No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response appears in the coverage.

All known accounts come from a single wire story datelined Chattanooga between November 25 and 27, which the New York Sun printed in full on November 26 under the headline "KU-KLUX IN TENNESSEE." Some editors sharpened the headline: the Omaha Bee wrote of "Negroes Charged With Trivial Offenses and Brutally Illtreated," and the Daily Kennebec Journal in Maine of "Respectable Negroes" tied to the stake. The text itself repeated the band's warning about "thieving neighbors" and described Molly Powell as a woman "whose reputation is not the best."

A shorter version, without the source's name or the other victims, ran on November 27 in the Memphis Appeal, the only Tennessee paper found, which closed with the line that the victims "have generally been accused of stealing." The same short version appeared that day in the Wheeling Intelligencer as "Intimidating Negroes," in the Indianapolis Journal and in the Wichita Eagle, and on November 29 twice in the Emporia Weekly News, while the Kenosha Telegraph-Courier reprinted the full text with all five victims.

Most versions place the attack "last week," but the Omaha Bee's copy says "a month ago." Likewise, the short version printed in Kansas said Smiley was "pretty badly scorched," where the fuller texts say only that the fire was kept off him and he was heated.

reader.title: Whipping of Hicks Smiley
bases: A band of about twenty 'regulators' that had chalked warning notices on Black residents' doors seized Smiley at his house, subjected him to a mock burning and whipped him, one of a series of night punishments by the same band (A1, A2, A3).

A 'score of men' acting without legal authority as self-styled regulators punished Smiley, but every version has him released and driven into his house alive after a whipping (A1, A2, A7); no killing is reported.
All versions descend from one Chattanooga wire report relaying the secondhand account of a traveling salesman, J. A. Johnston (A1, A2, A7); no local or independent report was found.

accounts.label: Traveling salesman's report (Chattanooga wire)
accounts.gist: A Chattanooga drummer said a band of regulators molesting only Black people had caused a panic in three Cumberland counties; a score of men tied Smiley to a tree, built a fire around him and whipped him.

framing.detail: The Sun headed the dispatch 'KU-KLUX IN TENNESSEE' and 'A Band of Regulators Terrifying Negroes in the Cumberland Valley', while repeating the band's 'thieving neighbors' warning and calling Molly Powell's reputation 'not the best'.
The Omaha Bee's headline read 'KUKLUX AGAIN. Negroes Charged With Trivial Offenses and Brutally Illtreated.'
The Kennebec Journal headed its version 'Respectable Negroes Who Are Tied to the Stake Whipped and Tarred and Feathered.'
The Memphis Appeal ran a shortened version, 'A Band of Men Spreading Terror Among Negroes', ending that the victims 'have generally been accused of stealing'.
The Wichita Eagle ran the short version under 'TENNESSEE REGULATORS'.
